section.sectionSummaryBrief: When Torah study lacks the awareness that it is God's Torah, it can lead to divisiveness and self-importance, as illustrated by a story of a scholar who complained to the Tzemach Tzedek about being trampled upon.
section.t: And from the continuation of the topics in the maamar it is understood,
that when the study of Torah is not in this manner,
then,
(in addition to the fact that it does not bring peace to the world)
it is possible that it will bring about division of hearts,
the opposite of peace.
For when he lacks the feeling that the Torah is the Torah of Havayah,
then,
he takes credit for himself that he studied much Torah43
and becomes a tangible entity that considers himself a man of virtue and an important person,
and this causes division of hearts,
for from the perspective of his selfhood he thinks that everything the other says or does is in order to oppose him.
And as the story
(cited in the maamar44),
that someone
(a great intellectual in scholarship)
came to the Tzemach Tzedek for a private audience and complained, "They are stepping on me in the study hall,"
and the Tzemach Tzedek answered him,
"You are spreading yourself over the entire study hall,
so wherever that one steps, it is all on you."
And it can be said,
that this which the maamar brings, that his claim was that they were trampling on him in the study hall,
that although the study hall is a micro-sanctuary45,
that the indwelling of the Shechinah in the micro-sanctuary is akin to the indwelling of the Shechinah in the Holy Temple46,
nevertheless,
even there there was the spreading of his selfhood.
And the maamar is precise,
that this complaint before the Tzemach Tzedek that they were trampling on him was when he was in a private audience,
that the matter of a private audience is the connection of the Yechidah of the one entering the private audience with the Yechidah of the Rebbe to whom he entered47,
and nevertheless,
even when he was in the private audience, he had the feeling that they were trampling on him.
And therefore the maamar brings the above details of the story,
in order to emphasize that through intellect alone,
without avodah,
it is possible for there to be a spreading of selfhood even in a micro-sanctuary and even when entering a private audience,
from which is understood the necessity of the matter of avodah.
And afterwards the Tzemach Tzedek told him the explanation of the verse48
"Let the wicked forsake his way and the man of iniquity his thoughts,"
"on"
(with a cholam)
is strength and power49,
and the explanation of "man of iniquity" is a man strong in his own opinion.
And this is "Let the wicked forsake his way and the man of iniquity his thoughts,"
that just as "let the wicked forsake his way" is something necessary,
for without teshuvah it is impossible to approach the holy,
so too it is necessary that the man of iniquity forsake his thoughts
(the thoughts of selfhood).

section.sectionSummaryBrief: The plural "thoughts" indicates that even the most subtle levels of self-oriented thought must be abandoned, as even a fine spiritual film on a Torah scholar acts as a barrier.
section.t: And it can be said,
that what is written "his thoughts" in the plural,
it is,
for in the thought of selfhood there are several levels,
and therefore it is stated "let him forsake... his thoughts" in the plural,
that he must forsake the subtle thought,
and even the most subtle of the subtle.
And to note,
from the statement of our sages of blessed memory50
regarding the matter of a film on a garment that interposes regarding immersion,
that of a builder
[these are Torah scholars who engage in the building of the world]
on one side and of a boor on two sides.
From this it is understood also regarding a spiritual film,
that in a Torah scholar even a subtle thought interposes,
and therefore it is necessary that he forsake "his thoughts" in the plural.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: The beginning of avodah is self-nullification, which enables both the upward approach through prayer and the downward approach through Torah, and this nullification brings complete peace.
section.t: And it is explained in the maamar51,
that the beginning of avodah is self-nullification.
For in order to draw near to Elokus,

both in the aspect of drawing near from below to above to ascend from level to level in prayer and in the aspect of drawing near from above to below in the attainment of Elokus in his soul through Torah,
it is through humility and lowliness.
And it can be said,
that this which the maamar specifies the two manners of drawing near to Elokus,
although in order to explain the language of the Targum "Alfin b'Oraisa d'Havayah" it seemingly only pertains to the drawing near through Torah,
it is in order to hint that through the precedence of self-nullification,
the peace of your children,
Torah scholars who engage in Torah
(from above to below),
is in completeness,
that it also includes the virtue of the peace of prayer
(from below to above)52.
